A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same function-word learning study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including v1 Appendices A–F and v2 Appendices A–I.

before.justification: V1 reports original analyses of 186 languages, GPT-2 experiments on manipulated English corpora, BLiMP results, attention probing, and ablations.

after.justification: V2 reports original corpus and modeling results, including revised transformer results and additional 5-gram comparisons, interaction experiments, language-recognition scores, and attention-entropy analyses.

M1.justification: The GPT-2 architecture, individual corpus transformations, function-word inventory, attention probe, and masking/deletion procedures are retained. The additional work combines existing manipulations and adds comparison models and diagnostic experiments rather than redesigning the core method.

E1.justification: The 186-language survey and core English Wikipedia/BLiMP coverage remain. V2 adds three combined-manipulation scenarios and a seven-way language-variant recognition task. A UD-CHILDES comparison replaces v1's BabyLM sentence-length and complexity comparison.

E2.justification: V1 compares transformer models across language conditions. V2 introduces an evaluated alternative model family: KenLM 5-gram models with Kneser-Ney smoothing, reported alongside transformers in Table 2 and the interaction experiments. This adds a substantive control for explanations based on local statistical patterns.

E3.justification: V2 adds seven-way forced-choice evaluation, combined-condition comparisons using transformer seed 53, and an entropy metric for attention-head concentration. These introduce distinct evaluation procedures; the stated core GPT-2 hyperparameters, corpus splits, and BLiMP filtering remain unchanged.

E4.justification: New Appendices G–I investigate language-variant competence, interactions among frequency, structure, and boundary alignment, and quantitative attention-head concentration across seeds. These substantially extend v1's probing and masking/deletion analyses. The additional-seed visualizations themselves already existed in v1.

E5.justification: V2 replaces the main comparison's isolated paired t-test with a mixed-effects analysis, adds significance tests for deletion and masking, and reports attention-entropy means, standard deviations, and per-seed values. The main experiments still report three seeds; these additions do not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: Table 2 extensively revises reported accuracies: NATURALFUNCTION changes from 67.3 to 72.7 and MOREFUNCTION from 58.5 to 69.7, reversing the relative penalties associated with frequency and structural association. Figures 4–6 also change substantially. V2 adds 5-gram, recognition, interaction, and entropy results; the PDFs do not explain the broad numerical revisions through changed core training settings.

T1.justification: The dependency-entropy calculations and Appendix E probing equations retain their mathematical substance. V2 clarifies conditional-entropy notation and explicitly writes the existing boundary-rate calculation, without adding or revising theoretical results, assumptions, or proofs.

C1.justification: V1 prominently claims frequency contributes more than structural association, which contributes more than boundary alignment. V2's results summary and conclusion instead identify structural association as strongest. It also replaces the headline emphasis on similar performance arising from different mechanisms with acquisition-to-processing reliance and generalization beyond n-gram heuristics.

C2.justification: V2 revises the interpretations of attention specialization and MOREFUNCTION's masking sensitivity, and adds explanations based on the new controls. Its limitations newly discuss pseudo-word randomness and BLiMP's inability to exclude surface heuristics. It also removes v1's explicit hypothesis that the reported cue hierarchy generalizes beyond English.

D1.justification: V2 adds tokenizer training-split information, KenLM implementation details, and settings for the interaction experiments, and updates the code repository location. The existing GPT-2 hyperparameters, hardware, split sizes, and seed list are retained.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 substantially expands positioning within controlled corpus manipulation and filtered-corpus training, adding works such as Kallini et al. and Patil et al. The discussion also broadens its grounding in learning biases and cultural evolution, while several earlier general computational-modeling references disappear.

P1.justification: V2 shortens the title and extensively rewrites the abstract, research questions, results narratives, conclusion, and limitations. It moves the cross-linguistic analysis ahead of modeling and integrates the former standalone methodology into the modeling section, substantially reorganizing the argument.

P2.justification: Table 2 gains a 5-gram column, Table 7 gains interaction conditions, and Figures 1 and 3 gain treebank labels. Figure 5 is compressed and rescaled. New Figure 7 and Tables 9–12 introduce interaction plots, diagnostic results, entropy summaries, and transformed examples, alongside substantial relocation of existing displays.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful 5-gram controls, interaction tests, statistical reporting, and more specific limitations. However, broad result revisions remain unexplained, and new stability claims conflict with Tables 10–11: NATURALFUNCTION's standard deviation exceeds four alternatives, and seed 67 does not consistently have the highest entropy. These unresolved reliability issues prevent a confident judgment that the added evidence produces a net quality improvement.
